## The Question
Airbnb is a platform that connects travelers looking for short-term accomodations with property owners interested in renting out their property; Airbnb listings can be found on [aribnb.com](airbnb.com). [insideairbnb.com](https://insideairbnb.com) is a website which gathers data on airbnb listings in selected locations by periodically scraping airbnb.com search results for those areas. Scraped information for each listing contains data on the the host (i.e. the property owner), the accomodation, and user reviews; data from the scrapings is made available in the form of datasets collecting both raw variables, and calculated fields at [insideaibnb.com](https://insideairbnb.com).

In this analysis I will work with data for Airbnb listings in Oslo. The main focus will be the price per night, and the features of the airbnb listings. In particular, the analysis aims to answer 3 main questions:

-  What are the main drivers of the price per night?
-  How much does the location of the accomodation impact the price per night, and how much do accomodations in different locations differ from one another?
-  Do the (recorded) host's features have any relation to the price per night or to the features of the accomodation? 

## Getting the Data

Data on Airbnb Locations in Oslo obtained from [insideairbnb.com](https://insideairbnb.com/get-the-data/). The data were gathered by the platform through a web scraping of [airbnb.com](https://www.airbnb.com/); in total `{r} nrow(osloairbnb)` listings were scraped on `{r} osloairbnb$last_scraped |> unique() |> length()` unique dates. @tbl-last-scrape reports the dates on which the scraping occurred and the numbers of listing scraped on each date. To allow for reproducibility, the dataset was sourced directly from the web and its version was pinned.  @fig-locations shows the location of all listings that were scraped across the various neighborhoods.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: "Dates of scraping and number of scraped listings."
#| label: tbl-last-scrape

#Understanding when each listing was scraped
num_scraped <- osloairbnb |>
  group_by(last_scraped) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  ungroup()
```

## A first look

```{r}
#| label: tbl-skim
#| tbl-cap: "A one-line summary of the dataset."
sk_osloairbnb <- skim_without_charts(osloairbnb)
print(sk_osloairbnb)

osloairbnb <- osloairbnb |>
  select(!ends_with("url") & !where(\(x) all(is.na(x))))
```

A summary of the dataset is shown in @tbl-skim. We see that for some variables all values are missing (complete_rate = 0). Those variables were dropped from the dataset altogether. Moreover, some variables only contained urls. Those variables were also dropped.

@fig-missing shows missing values among variables having at least one missing values.
```{r}
#| label: fig-missing
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Missing values across variables."
osloairbnb |>
  select(where(\(x) anyNA(x))) |>
  vis_miss() +
  theme(
    # Rotate text slightly, align the text ends perfectly to the ticks, and remove the massive gap
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, vjust = 1, hjust = 1)
  )
```

A considerable number of missing values can be seen for the following variables:
host_location, hos_about, bedrooms, beds, bathrooms, variables relating to price, and variables relating to revies. Interestingly, the variable bathrooms_text has almost no missing values, meaning that most missing values in bathrooms are just a byproduct of the scraping, and can be filled in easily. Moreover, is seems that missingness in variables relating to price, and in variables relating to reviews tends to occur simultaneously; @fig-missing-2 provides a visualization of missingness patterns in these variables. It seems that when there are missing values, in general, either all price variables are missing or all review variables are missing, but only relatively rarely both are missing together.

```{r}
#| label: fig-missing-2
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Patterns in missingness across price, review, and host infotmation variables"

pat_matrix <- osloairbnb |>
  select(where(\(x) anyNA(x)) & (starts_with("price") | contains("review"))) |>
  mice::md.pattern(plot = FALSE)
raw_counts <- as.numeric(rownames(pat_matrix)[-nrow(pat_matrix)])

# 3. Convert raw counts to rounded percentage strings
pct_labels <- paste0(round((raw_counts / nrow(osloairbnb)) * 100, 1), "%")

osloairbnb |>
  select(where(\(x) anyNA(x)) & (starts_with("price") | contains("review"))) |>
  ggmice::plot_pattern(square = FALSE, rotate = TRUE) +
  scale_y_reverse(
    breaks = seq_along(raw_counts),
    labels = pct_labels,
    sec.axis = dup_axis(name = "Number of missing entries\nper pattern")
  ) +
  labs(y = "Pattern frequency (%)")
```

## Cleaning decisions {#sec-cleaning}
From @tbl-skim, we see a lot of variables are coded in an unsuitable way. For instance, many ids are coded as numeric, dates are coded as character, prices are coded as character, and binary variables are coded as logical. I will now clean the data to fix the issues.

```{r}
osloairbnb <- osloairbnb |>
  mutate(
    across(ends_with("id"), as_factor),
    across(ends_with("type"), as_factor),
    across(where(\(x) is.logical(x)), \(y) {
      factor(y, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c("Yes", "No"))
    }),
    across(contains(c("last", "first", "date")), as_date),
    across(starts_with("price_"), as.numeric),
    source = as_factor(source)
  )
```

All id variables were recoded as factors; property type and room type were also recoded as factors; all logical variables were recoded as factors; the variable source, indicating the scrape that provided the data, was also recoded as a factor; finally, variables indicating dates, e.g. last_scraped, last_review, and price_quote_checkin_date, were recoded as the appropriate data type.

Apart from that, some variables can be created starting from the existing ones. Namely, the bathrooms_text variable can be used to fill in the missing values for the bathrooms variable, and the amenities variable can be used to create multiple dummy variables indicating whether an accomodation offers a certain amenity or not, so as to provide a better gauge of the features of the accomodations.

```{r}
osloairbnb$bathrooms_new <- osloairbnb$bathrooms_text |> #Creating new factor variable for the number of bathrooms
  strsplit(" ") |> #splitting bathrooms_text values
  vapply(\(x) x[1], character(1)) #Extracting 1st element of each of the split values
```

In creating the new bathrooms variable (bathrooms_new) starting from bathrooms_text, `{r} sum(grepl("0", osloairbnb$bathrooms_new, ignore.case = T))` were recorded as having 0 bathrooms. Thes values will be recoded as NAs.
The column will then be recoded as numeric

```{r}
osloairbnb <- osloairbnb |>
  mutate(bathrooms_new = if_else(bathrooms_new == "0", NA, bathrooms_new)) |> #Replacing 0 values with NAs
  mutate(
    bathrooms_new = if_else(
      grepl("Half|Shared|Private", bathrooms_new, ignore.case = TRUE),
      "0.5",
      bathrooms_new
    )
  ) |> #Catching half bathrooms and replacing with 0.5
  mutate(bathrooms_new = as.numeric(bathrooms_new))
```

Now, before creating dummy variables for the amenities, let us consider which amenities are most common. It would be sensible to only keep track of amenities that are not too rare but, at the same time, not so common that (almost) every accomodation has them: such features would not provide much information.

To visualize the frequency of amenities across all accomodations, we will start with a simple word cloud, shown in @fig-wordcloud. The purpose of this wordcloud is to help us understand what amenities are offered across listings, in a rough but quick way. The wordcloud only shows amenities that are present in more than 10% but less than in 90% of listings. Considering  all amenities would be cumbersome; furthermore, some amenities are likely to be provided by all accomodations, but only be mentioned by part of the listings, or be mentioned using different wordings, (e.g. hot water or heating). For this analysis, we will thus focus only on a selection of amenities which could reasonably be related to the price of an accomodation and/or may be influenced by the location of the airbnb. If one were interested in other amenities, the code could be easily modified to take them into account.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wordcloud
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 12
#| fig-cap: "Wordcloud of amenities. The size of the words is proportional to the percentage of homes having that amenity. Amenities present in over 90% of homes or in less than 10% of homes were excluded"
#| warning: true

withr::local_seed(1234)

amenities_vec <- osloairbnb$amenities |>
  str_to_lower() |>
  str_split(",", simplify = TRUE) |>
  str_replace_all("[:punct:]+", " ") |>
  str_replace_all("u([0-9a-fA-F]{4})", "") |> #removing scraping artefacts
  str_trim()

amenities_vec <- amenities_vec[amenities_vec != ""]

amenities_freqs <- (table(amenities_vec) / nrow(osloairbnb)) |> as_tibble() #For a better visualization we will use percentage frequencies.

#We remove amenities present in over 90% of apartments and in at least 5%
amenities_freqs <- amenities_freqs[
  amenities_freqs$n <= .90 & amenities_freqs$n >= .1,
]

ggwordcloud::ggwordcloud(
  words = amenities_freqs$amenities_vec,
  freq = amenities_freqs$n,
  min.freq = 0,
  scale = c(3.5, 1),
  colors = paletteer::paletteer_d("poisonfrogs::Amacero")
)
```

We will focus on the following amenities: bed linens, parking (absent/free/paid), pets allowed, bed linens, host greeting, outdoor dining area, private patio or balcony, bbq grill, long term stays allowed, and air conditioning. To that end, we will create a dummy variable for each amenity, for each listing.

```{r}
osloairbnb <- osloairbnb |>
  mutate(
    pets_allowed = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "pets allowed"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    bed_linens = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "bed linens"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    host_greeting = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "host greets you"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    outdoor_dining = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "outdoor dining area"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    private_patio = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "private patio or balcony"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    bbq_grill = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), "bbq grill|barbecue"),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    paid_parking = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), regex("\\bpaid\\b[^\"]*parking", ignore_case = TRUE)),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
    free_parking = if_else(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(amenities), regex("\\bfree\\b[^\"]*parking", ignore_case = TRUE)),
      "yes",
      "no"
    ),
  )
```
